newsitem.title: GERMANY: Insurer Gerling tots up Euro, 2000 costs.
newsitem.headline: Insurer Gerling tots up Euro, 2000 costs.

text.p: German insurer Gerling said the introduction of the single European currency will cost it between 40 and 50 million marks in changes to its computer systems alone.
The changeover to the date 2000 will cost between 15 million and 20 million marks, Norbert Heinen, member of the management board of Gerling Lebensversicherung, said.
Heinen is also a managing director of GKI, the Gerling subsidiary running the group's computer systems.
"The current government tax reform plans could cost us at least another 10 million marks, but this is difficult to estimate, as the proposals are not yet very detailed," he said.
Those three problems alone would cost Gerling half of its annual programme development capacity, he said.
The Euro could create special problems for Gerling as a large industrial insurer, said Heinen.

"We believe that private customers will stick to the deutschemark as long as possible. But we cannot rule out that our industrial customers might want us to administer their contracts in Euro as from 1 January 1999," he said.
Gerling would avoid a "big bang" conversion.

"If systems are changed over gradually, you need to operate with both currencies for some time. The costs of the changeover depend to a large degree on the extent to which you need dual operation, whether for external purposes only or also for all internal operations."
Gerling had not taken a final decision on that, he added.
The changeover from 1999 to the date 2000 was also creating problems.

"Like most insurers, we have numerous older programmes which operate with two-digit years," said Heinen. As those programmes cannot differentiate between years in the 20th and 21st centuries, they need to be changed.
"Our program code runs to 12 million lines, which all have to be searched and corrected, including the various links," he said.
